title: Earning more but keeping less? How to maximise your income
html:
Stuart Garlick, regional manager at Wesleyan Financial Services, explores how to maximise your income, manage your tax position and build long-term financial security.

As a dentist, moving from NHS dentistry to private practice can offer the opportunity to take more control of your earning potential. But while increasing your income is an understandable goal, how much of what you earn are you actually keeping?

A higher income can offer more financial freedom, but there are other factors to consider. For example, you’ll need to think about any new costs associated with the move, as well as the impact on your tax circumstances.

Without a clear plan, it’s easy to find that your increased earnings aren’t working as hard towards your financial goals as you’d originally hoped.

Look beyond headline income

When you transition to private dentistry, it’s natural to focus on what you could earn. But your headline income is only one part of the picture.

Your take home pay will depend on many factors, including your:

  • Working arrangements
  • Business expenses
  • Tax position
  • Pension contributions.

Remember too, income can fluctuate, especially when you’re establishing a private patient base or investing in your practice.

Make tax planning part of the picture

Depending on your individual circumstances, transitioning to private dentistry could affect the amount of tax you pay and the allowances available to you.

With this in mind, it’s important to understand your position rather than assuming an increase in earnings will translate directly into an increase in disposable income.

Working with an accountant can help you understand your tax liabilities and meet your obligations. A financial adviser can then help you assess how your income, pension contributions, savings and investments fit into your wider financial plans.

Let’s take pension contributions and ISAs as an example. Many offer tax advantages depending on your circumstances, but that doesn’t automatically mean it’s the right approach for you. You’ll need to consider your goals and income, as well as access to other financial resources.

Remember, the aim isn’t just to minimise tax. It’s to make informed decisions about your money while still keeping your wider financial priorities in view.

Tax treatment depends on your individual circumstances and may be subject to change in future.

Don’t let lifestyle spending absorb the difference

When your earnings increase, it can be tempting to increase your lifestyle spending too. Whether it’s a bigger home, a new car or more holidays, enjoying the rewards of your hard work is important.

However, if every increase in your income is matched by an increase in your spending, you could miss an opportunity to strengthen your financial position.

A useful starting point is to decide in advance how you want to use any additional income. You might choose to allocate some of it towards enjoying life now, while still directing a portion of it towards your savings and pension contributions.

There isn’t a one-size-fits-all approach for every dentist. What matters is finding a balance that allows you to enjoy your current lifestyle without losing sight of your longer-term ambitions.

Turn higher earnings into lasting financial security

Building wealth isn’t only about how much you earn. It’s also about what you choose to do with the money available to you.

If your income increases when you move into private dentistry, think about how that additional money could strengthen your financial foundations.

For example:

Build an emergency fund

Having accessible savings can help you manage unexpected costs or periods of reduced income. It also means you may reduce the need to rely on borrowing or disrupt your longer-term investments.

Review your pension arrangements

If moving away from NHS dentistry is going to affect your future pension provision, you may need to think about how you’ll continue building your retirement savings. Reviewing any existing NHS pension benefits alongside your private pension arrangements can help you figure out whether you’re on track to achieve your desired retirement income.

Consider your protection needs

Would you and your family be financially secure if your circumstances changed? If your income is used to meet household expenses (such as mortgage payments), it’s wise to review your income protection and insurance arrangements to make sure you can cover your regular outgoings.

Invest with your goals in mind

Depending on your circumstances, you may want to explore ways to invest for the long-term. Your investment strategy should reflect your time horizon, attitude to risk and capacity for loss.

Remember that investment values can fall as well as rise, and you may get back less than you invest.

Taking these steps can help turn your increased earnings into more financial resilience and choice over your future.

Give your financial plan room to evolve

Your financial priorities are likely to change throughout your career. When you start out, you may be focused on your income and building a financial safety net. As your career progresses, your priorities might turn into pension contributions, investing, supporting loved ones or planning an exit from practice ownership.

This is why it’s important to review your financial arrangements regularly, especially if there are significant changes to your circumstances. A financial plan shouldn’t be something you put in place once and then forget about. It should evolve alongside your career, helping you make informed choices for both your current and future needs.

Make your money work as hard as you do

Private dentistry may give you the opportunity to increase your earnings, but financial success isn’t measured by income alone. It’s about making your money work towards the life you want to live, both during your dental career and once you’ve stopped working.

A financial adviser who understands the dental profession can help you bring these different elements together, giving you a clearer picture of where you stand and how you could work towards your financial goals.
